title: Is Medicare Free? What You'll Pay in 2026

sections.text: Is Medicare Free? The Short Answer

sections.content: No, Medicare is not free for most people. Some parts can have no monthly premium depending on your work history, but almost everyone pays something, whether that's a premium, a deductible, coinsurance, or a combination of all three.

What you actually pay depends on which parts of Medicare you choose, how many years you or your spouse paid Medicare payroll taxes, and your household income. Two people on Medicare can have very different monthly costs based on these factors alone.
Knowing these costs ahead of time gives you a clearer picture of what to budget for and helps you compare coverage options with more confidence, rather than being surprised by a bill later.

sections.text: Why So Many People Believe Medicare Is Free

sections.content: Part of the confusion comes from mixing up Medicare with Medicaid. Medicaid is a state and federal program based on income that can cover care at little to no cost for those who qualify. Medicare is a federal health insurance program tied to age or disability, not income, and it isn't designed to be free.

Another source of confusion is payroll taxes. During your working years, you and your employer paid Medicare taxes from your paycheck, but those taxes only fund part of the program's costs, mainly Part A. They don't cover your ongoing premiums, deductibles, or coinsurance once you're enrolled.

Because most people don't pay a monthly premium for Part A, some assume the rest of Medicare works the same way. It doesn't. Part B, Part D, and any supplemental coverage you add typically come with their own separate costs.

sections.text: Medicare Part A Costs: Hospital Coverage

sections.content: You qualify for premium-free Part A if you or your spouse paid Medicare taxes for at least 10 years (40 quarters) of work. If you don't meet that threshold, you'll pay a monthly premium for Part A coverage.

Even with premium-free Part A, you're responsible for a deductible each benefit period, which is different from the annual deductibles you may be used to with other insurance. A benefit period starts when you're admitted to a hospital and ends after you've gone 60 days in a row without inpatient care, so you could pay the deductible more than once in a year if you're hospitalized multiple times with a gap between stays.

items: Part A deductible: $1,736 per benefit period in 2026
Hospital coinsurance: $434 per day for days 61 to 90, and $868 per day for lifetime reserve days beyond that
Skilled nursing facility coinsurance: $217 per day after day 20 of a covered stay
Part A premium for those who don't qualify for premium-free coverage: up to $565 per month in 2026, or $311 per month with 30 to 39 quarters of work

sections.calloutText: Because the Part A deductible applies per benefit period rather than per year, a short hospital stay followed by readmission after a break of 60 or more days could mean paying the deductible twice.

sections.text: Medicare Part B Costs: Doctor Visits and Outpatient Care

sections.content: Part B covers doctor visits, outpatient services, and preventive care, and nearly everyone pays a monthly premium for it. The standard Part B premium is $202.90 per month in 2026.

Before Medicare starts paying its share, you'll need to meet the annual Part B deductible of $283 in 2026. After that, you typically pay 20% coinsurance for most Part B services, with no annual cap on this out-of-pocket amount under Original Medicare alone.

If your income is above certain thresholds, you'll pay an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount, known as IRMAA, on top of the standard premium. This surcharge is based on your reported income from two years prior, meaning your 2026 premium is determined by your 2024 tax return. For individuals earning more than $109,000 or married couples filing jointly earning more than $218,000, [IRMAA surcharges apply to Part B premiums](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/medicare-costs), with total monthly premiums ranging from $284.10 up to $689.90 depending on income level.

Medicare Advantage plan premiums vary widely by plan and location, and some plans advertise $0 monthly premiums. Even with a $0 premium plan, you still pay your Part B premium, since Medicare Advantage replaces Original Medicare but doesn't eliminate that cost.

Beyond the premium, you'll likely pay copays for doctor visits, coinsurance for certain services, and other costs that vary by plan. Every Medicare Advantage plan has an annual out-of-pocket maximum, capped at $9,250 in 2026, which limits what you'll pay for covered services in a year once you reach it.

A low or $0 premium can look appealing, but it doesn't tell you the whole story. Comparing plans means looking at the total expected cost, including copays for the specific doctors and services you use regularly, not just the advertised premium.

When you're comparing Medicare Advantage plans, don't stop at the premium. Pull up the plan's Summary of Benefits and check the copay for a specialist visit, the cost tier for any drug you take regularly, and the out-of-pocket maximum side by side. A $0 premium plan with high specialist copays can end up costing more over a year than a plan with a modest premium and lower cost-sharing.

sections.text: Medicare Part D Costs: Prescription Drug Coverage

sections.content: Part D plans charge their own monthly premium, which averages $34.50 in 2026, though this varies by plan and insurer. Plans can also have an annual deductible, capped at $615 in 2026, before coverage kicks in for your prescriptions.

Once you've met the deductible, what you pay for each prescription depends on which tier it falls into on the plan's formulary, with copays or coinsurance generally increasing from lower tiers (generics) to higher tiers (brand-name and specialty drugs).

A major change from the Inflation Reduction Act continues in 2026: once your out-of-pocket drug spending reaches [the catastrophic coverage threshold of $2,100](https://www.cms.gov/), you pay nothing more for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the year. This cap gives people with high prescription costs a predictable ceiling on their annual spending.

Before enrolling in any Part D or Medicare Advantage plan with drug coverage, check the plan's formulary to confirm your specific medications are covered and see which tier they fall into. A plan that looks affordable on paper can turn out to be expensive if your prescriptions sit in a high-cost tier or aren't covered at all.

sections.text: Medigap and Other Costs That Affect Your Total Budget

sections.content: Medigap, also called Medicare Supplement insurance, charges its own monthly premium in exchange for covering some or all of the gaps left by Original Medicare, such as Part A and Part B coinsurance or deductibles, depending on which plan letter you choose.

Medigap only works alongside Original Medicare. It cannot be used with a Medicare Advantage plan, so if you're comparing Original Medicare plus Medigap against a Medicare Advantage plan, you're really comparing two different cost structures, not just two premiums.

A few other costs can catch people off guard if they miss certain deadlines. If you don't sign up for Part B when you're first eligible and don't have other qualifying coverage, you may face a [late enrollment penalty added to your premium](https://www.ssa.gov/) for as long as you have Part B. A similar penalty applies to Part D if you go without creditable drug coverage for 63 days or more after your initial enrollment window.

sections.calloutText: Late enrollment penalties for Part B and Part D are generally permanent additions to your premium, not one-time fees, so missing your enrollment window can raise your costs for as long as you're enrolled.

sections.text: How to Plan Your Medicare Budget Without Guessing

sections.content: Rather than estimating costs in the abstract, a few concrete steps can help you build a realistic Medicare budget based on your own situation.

items: List your current prescriptions and the doctors or specialists you see regularly, since this determines which plans make sense for you.
Estimate your expected care needs for the coming year, including any scheduled procedures or ongoing treatments.
Compare plan costs side by side, including premiums, deductibles, copays, and out-of-pocket maximums, not just the monthly price.
Check whether you qualify for assistance programs like Medicare Savings Programs or Extra Help, which can lower your premiums or drug costs if your income and resources fall within certain limits.

sections.content: Once you have this information gathered, speaking with a licensed Medicare agent can help you walk through actual numbers based on your doctors, prescriptions, and budget, without any obligation to enroll on the spot.
Comparing total cost, including premiums plus expected out-of-pocket spending, rather than focusing on the premium alone, is what prevents surprise bills after you've already enrolled.

faqs.question: I want to understand my costs before I talk to anyone. Where should I start?
faqs.answer: Start by reviewing an article like this one alongside the official cost tools at Medicare.gov, which let you look up specific plan costs in your area. Once you have a general sense of your options, you can reach out to a licensed agent when you're ready, with no obligation to decide right away.

faqs.question: Will I get a pushy sales call if I ask about Medicare costs?
faqs.answer: Licensed Medicare agents are there to answer your questions and explain your options clearly, not to pressure you into a decision. A reputable agent will walk through your specific costs and coverage needs and let you take the time you need to decide.

faqs.question: Can I just figure out these costs on my own?
faqs.answer: Yes, it's possible to research Medicare costs on your own using official resources. That said, plan details, premiums, and formularies change every year, so getting a second opinion from a licensed agent can help catch details you might overlook.

faqs.question: How do I know which cost information online is trustworthy?
faqs.answer: Rely on official sources like Medicare.gov, SSA.gov, and licensed Medicare agents for accurate cost information. Be cautious of unsourced claims, outdated figures, or sites that don't clearly explain where their numbers come from.

sections.text: Getting Clarity on Your Medicare Costs

sections.content: Medicare involves real costs across every part, from premiums and deductibles to coinsurance and potential penalties. Understanding these pieces in advance is what prevents unexpected bills once you're enrolled and using your coverage.

The most useful comparison is one built around your own doctors, prescriptions, and budget, rather than a generic look at premiums alone. Your costs will look different from a neighbor's or a family member's based on your specific health needs and income.

When you're ready, speaking with a licensed Medicare agent can give you a no-pressure cost comparison tailored to your situation, so you can choose coverage with a clearer sense of what you'll actually pay.

keyTakeaways: Most people do not pay a monthly premium for Part A if they or a spouse paid Medicare taxes for at least 10 years (40 quarters)
Nearly everyone pays a monthly premium for Part B, which is $202.90 in 2026, plus a $283 annual deductible
Part B coinsurance is typically 20% with no annual out-of-pocket cap under Original Medicare alone
Higher-income beneficiaries pay an IRMAA surcharge based on income reported two years prior
